title: Writing practice: The Cracked Bowl, Shadows and Trade Routes
description: Eight short writing tasks: retell a story with a problem and solution, correct a math answer, explain a shadow, pick a trade route, explain how to borrow a book, argue about books and movies, give directions, and write about the Moon.

stimuli.title: Story: The Cracked Bowl
paragraphs: Nia lived with her grandmother, who kept a blue clay bowl on the kitchen shelf. One afternoon, Nia reached for an orange and her elbow hit the bowl. It fell and broke into four pieces. Nia’s heart pounded. She hid the pieces in a cloth bag under her bed.

All evening, Nia felt a heavy worry in her stomach. At dinner she could hardly eat. Finally, she took out the bag and carried it to her grandmother. “I am so sorry,” she whispered. Her grandmother looked at the pieces and did not shout. “Thank you for telling me the truth,” she said. “A bowl can be mended.”

The next day they glued the pieces together. The bowl had thin lines where it had broken. Nia felt lighter than she had in days. Her grandmother put the bowl back on the shelf and placed an orange inside it.

stimuli.title: Math problem: Vans for a field trip
paragraphs: A school has 36 students going on a field trip. Each van holds 8 students.
Marcus wrote: “36 ÷ 8 = 4 with a remainder of 4, so we need 4 vans.”

stimuli.title: Data table: Shadow of a stick
stimuli.caption: A 100 cm stick was placed straight up in the schoolyard. Students measured its shadow three times in one day. The Sun moves across the sky during the day. A shadow is longer when the Sun is low in the sky and shorter when the Sun is high.

stimuli.title: Table: Three routes to the market town
stimuli.caption: Merchants in an invented kingdom want to carry pottery from their workshop to a market town.
rows: Steep roads and snow in winter
Calm water and landing docks along the way
No fresh water for six days

stimuli.title: Poster: Borrowing a class book
paragraphs: A new student joins your class. This poster hangs next to the bookshelf.

Borrowing a Class Book. 1. Choose a book from the shelf. 2. Write your name and the book title on the clipboard sheet. 3. Put a bookmark in the book where you stop reading. 4. When you finish, put the book back on the same shelf and cross out your name.

stimuli.title: Two viewpoints: Book or movie?
paragraphs: Two students were asked: “Which is better for enjoying a story, reading the book or watching the movie?”
Hana says: “Books are better. When you read, you imagine the characters and places in your own mind. A book also gives details that a movie leaves out. You can stop to think whenever you want.”
Luis says: “Movies are better. You see the story come alive right away. A movie shows places you may never have visited. It also takes about two hours, but a long book can take weeks.”

stimuli.title: Map in words: The school hallway
paragraphs: A long hallway goes from the front door at the south end to the art room at the north end.
On the west side, from south to north, are the office, Room 3, and Room 5. On the east side, from south to north, are the nurse’s room, the library, and Room 6.
A new student is standing at the front door, facing north.
When you face north, east is on your right and west is on your left.

stimuli.title: Fact card: The Moon
stimuli.caption: Facts about the Moon.
rows: The Moon does not make its own light. It reflects light from the Sun.
It has craters, which are bowl-shaped holes made when rocks hit it.
The Moon has almost no air.

items.stem: Retell the story “The Cracked Bowl” in your own words. Include the problem, how Nia’s feelings changed, and how the problem was solved.

checklist: I told the problem.
I told the events in order.
I told how Nia felt before and after she told the truth.
I told how the problem was solved.
I used time words and past-tense verbs.
exemplar: Task completion: retells the problem (the broken bowl), Nia’s hiding of the pieces, her confession, and the repair.
Development: shows the change in Nia’s feelings (worried, then relieved) with details.
Organization: clear beginning, middle, and end with time words.
Language: past-tense verbs, varied sentence structures, and pronoun reference are controlled.
Cohesion: transitions such as after that, finally, and the next day.

support.clue: Find the sentences that tell how Nia feels at three points: after the crash, at dinner, and after the repair. What causes each feeling?
support.frame: At the beginning, ______. The problem was that ______. Nia felt ______ because ______. Then ______. Finally, ______. After that, Nia felt ______ because ______. The problem was solved when ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different story. “At the beginning, Mina planned a picnic. The problem was that it started to rain. Mina felt disappointed because she had made sandwiches. Then her dad had an idea. Finally, they spread a blanket on the living room floor. After that, Mina felt cheerful because the picnic still happened. The problem was solved when they changed the place.” Notice how the writer tells the problem, the feeling, and the solution in order.

Retell your story in the same way.

items.stem: Is Marcus’s answer correct? Write a claim and support it with math. Explain what the remainder means and how many vans are needed.

checklist: I told whether Marcus is correct.
I used the numbers 36, 8, and the remainder in my math.
I explained what the remainder means for the students.
I told how many vans are needed.
I used words such as because, so, and therefore.
exemplar: Task completion: claims that Marcus is not correct and states that 5 vans are needed.
Math accuracy: 4 vans hold 4 × 8 = 32 students; 36 − 32 = 4 students remain, so another van is needed.
Reasoning: interprets the remainder in the context (4 students still need a ride).
Vocabulary: remainder, divide, hold, enough.
Language: complex sentences with because and so.

support.clue: Check Marcus’s plan: how many students can 4 vans hold in all? What happens to the students who are left?
support.frame: I claim that Marcus is ______ . Four vans can carry ______ × ______ = ______ students. That is not enough because ______. The remainder of ______ means that ______. Therefore, the school needs ______ vans.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different problem. “A baker puts 5 muffins in each box and has 23 muffins. A student wrote that 4 boxes are enough. I claim that the answer is not correct. Four boxes hold 4 × 5 = 20 muffins. That is not enough because 3 muffins are left. The remainder of 3 means that those muffins need another box. Therefore, the baker needs 5 boxes.” Notice that the writer explains what the remainder means.

Write your claim about the vans in the same way.

facts: 36 ÷ 8 = 4 remainder 4
5 vans can hold 40 students, which is enough for 36 students.
Model: 4 × 5 = 20 and 23 − 20 = 3; 5 boxes hold 25 muffins.

items.stem: Explain why the shadow was shortest at midday. Use numbers from the table and tell where the Sun was in the sky.

checklist: I used numbers from the table.
I told where the Sun was in the morning and at midday.
I explained why the shadow changed.
I used the word because or so.
exemplar: Task completion: states the shadow was shortest at midday (20 cm) and explains the Sun was high in the sky.
Reasoning: connects the Sun’s position to the length of the shadow.
Evidence: uses at least two numbers from the table.
Vocabulary: shadow, Sun, sky, midday.

support.clue: Compare the three shadow lengths. Think about how high the Sun is when the shadow is short and when it is long.
support.frame: The shadow was shortest at ______, when it was ______ cm. In the morning, the Sun was ______ in the sky, so the shadow was ______. At midday, the Sun was ______, so the shadow was ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different topic. “The candle was shortest at 9 p.m., when it was 4 cm tall. At 6 p.m., it was 12 cm tall. The flame used up the wax all evening, so the candle lost height. As a result, it was shortest at night.” Notice that the writer uses numbers and then gives the reason.

Explain your shadow data in the same way.

facts: The Sun is highest in the sky around midday, so shadows are shortest then.
The Sun is lower in the sky in the morning and late afternoon, so shadows are longer.
The shadow lengths in the table are invented for this practice.
A burning candle uses up its wax, so it gets shorter (used in the mentor example only).

items.stem: Which route should the merchants choose to carry pottery to the market town? Make a claim and support it with evidence from the table.

checklist: I wrote which route I choose.
I used at least two facts from the table.
I told why another route is not as good.
I used words such as because and however.
exemplar: Task completion: chooses a route and supports the choice with two or more table details.
Reasoning: explains why the facts matter for carrying pottery (for example, calm water protects pots).
Counterpoint: explains why at least one other route is a worse choice.
Language: connectors because, however, and since.
Note: more than one choice can be defensible if it is supported by evidence.

support.clue: Compare the rows on distance, travel time, and what the merchants face. Think about what matters most when carrying pottery.
support.frame: I think the merchants should take the ______ because ______. The table shows that ______. In addition, ______. The ______ is not as good because ______. For these reasons, ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different choice. “I think the family should take the train because it is faster. The schedule shows that the train takes 3 hours, but the bus takes 5 hours. In addition, the train has seats with tables. The bus is not as good because it stops many times. For these reasons, the train is the better choice.” Notice that the writer compares the two options.

Write your claim about the routes in the same way.

facts: Travel times: 12 days, 9 days, and 14 days; distances: 300 km, 450 km, and 280 km.
The river route takes the least time even though it is the longest distance.
The route data is invented for this practice.

items.stem: Explain to the new student how to borrow and return a class book. Tell each step in your own words and tell why one step is important.

checklist: I told all the steps in order.
I used sequence words such as first, next, then, and finally.
I told why one step is important.
I wrote in my own words.
exemplar: Task completion: includes all four steps, in order, and a reason for one step.
Language: uses sequence words and clear command or statement forms (you should, you write).
Reasoning: gives a reason using because or so.
Clarity: the new student could follow the directions.
Organization: steps are separated by sequence words.

support.clue: Find the four numbered steps. Choose one step and ask yourself what would go wrong if people skipped it.
support.frame: To borrow a class book, first you ______. Next, you ______. Then you ______. Finally, when you finish, you ______. One important step is ______ because ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different process. “To use the class computer, first you sign your name on the list. Next, you wait for your turn. Then you log in with your class number. Finally, you log out. Logging out is important because it keeps your work private.” Notice the sequence words and the reason at the end.

Explain how to borrow a book in the same way.

items.stem: Which is better for enjoying a story, the book or the movie? Take a side. Use ideas from both students, and answer one reason from the other side.

checklist: I wrote my position in the first sentence.
I used at least two reasons.
I used an idea from Hana or Luis.
I answered one reason from the other side.
I ended with a closing sentence.
exemplar: Task completion: states a position and supports it with two or more reasons drawn from the text and the writer’s own thinking.
Counterargument: acknowledges one point from the other student and responds to it.
Organization: introduction, reasons, response to the other side, and conclusion.
Language: complex sentences and connectors such as although, however, and for example.
Evidence: reasons are explained, not just listed.

support.clue: Underline one reason in each student’s comment. Which reasons do you agree with most? Which reason from the other side can you answer?
support.frame: In my opinion, ______ is better for enjoying a story. One reason is that ______. For example, ______. In addition, ______. Although ______ says that ______, I disagree because ______. In conclusion, ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different question. “In my opinion, walking is better for getting to school. One reason is that it gives you fresh air. For example, you can hear birds and see the trees. In addition, it helps you wake up. Although some students say that the bus is faster, I disagree because the walk takes only ten minutes and the bus often waits at many stops. In conclusion, walking is a good way to start the day.” Notice that the writer answers the other side.

Write your opinion about books and movies in the same way.

facts: Hana says reading lets you imagine characters and stop to think.
Luis says a movie shows the story right away and takes about two hours, while a long book can take weeks.

items.stem: Write directions for the new student to get from the front door to the library. Use words like straight, left, right, past, and next to.

checklist: I told where to start.
I used direction words like straight, left, and right.
I mentioned the room to walk past.
I told which side the library is on.
exemplar: Task completion: tells how to reach the library (walk north past the nurse’s room; the library is on the right).
Accuracy: left and right match the map description for someone facing north.
Language: uses imperative sentences and position words such as past and next to.
Organization: steps in order.

support.clue: The student faces north. Which side is east? Which room comes first on that side, and which comes second?
support.frame: Start at ______. Walk ______ past the ______. The library is on your ______. It is ______ the ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different place. “Start at the classroom door. Walk straight to the end of the hall. Turn left at the water fountain. The cafeteria is on your right. It is next to the gym.” Notice the order of the steps and the position words.

Write your directions to the library in the same way.

facts: When facing north, east is on your right and west is on your left.
The library is the second room on the east side, after the nurse’s room.
The hallway map is invented for this practice.

items.stem: Write a short science paragraph about the Moon for younger students. Use at least three facts from the card.

checklist: I wrote a first sentence that tells the topic.
I used at least three facts from the card.
I wrote complete sentences.
I used science words such as craters and reflects.
exemplar: Task completion: includes a topic sentence and three accurate facts from the card.
Language: complete sentences with present-tense verbs.
Vocabulary: uses terms such as Moon, Earth, craters, and reflects.
Audience: simple, clear wording for younger students.

support.clue: Read each row. Choose three facts that you think younger students will find interesting, and decide which one to say first.
support.frame: The Moon is ______. It ______ around ______. The Moon does not ______, but it ______. Its surface has ______. Another fact is that ______.
support.model:
Mentor example about a different topic. “Rainbows are colorful arcs in the sky. They appear when sunlight shines through raindrops. A rainbow has many colors. Another fact is that you often see a rainbow when the Sun is behind you.” Notice the topic sentence and the facts.

Write about the Moon in the same way.

facts: The Moon moves around Earth.
The Moon does not make its own light; it reflects light from the Sun.
The Moon has craters made when rocks hit its surface.
The Moon has almost no air.
Model: a rainbow forms when sunlight passes through raindrops, and you see one with the Sun behind you.
